description: THERMYX is a two-person team from two countries. We’re building THERMYX, a unified 20-year wildfire history that merges NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite data into one fair timeline. The newer satellite sees smaller fires, so raw data shows a fake jump in 2012. We fix that, group detections into real fire events, and show it on an interactive globe with a Raw vs Fixed toggle.
summary:
For 20 years, NASA has watched fires from space with two instruments. MODIS began in 2000. VIIRS began in 2012, and it sees more. Put the two records side by side and fires seem to explode in 2012. They didn’t. The instrument improved.

THERMYX fixes that. It merges both records into one consistent timeline and shows Original and Fixed side by side. In California, the 2012 jump falls from about +134% to about +20% after correction. The same method now runs across six regions: California, Amazon, Australia, India, Malaysia, and Canada’s boreal forest. Every technical term comes with a plain-English line, so scientists, journalists, and policymakers can all read it.

Why India matters: many fires there are small, like crop-residue burning, and small fires are where the two sensors disagree most. A fair baseline lets people judge whether burning is really changing.

Validation against burned-area maps is in progress, so results are preliminary. Built by Team Two Orbits, across two countries. Data: NASA FIRMS.
details:
THERMYX merges NASA's two satellite fire records into one consistent timeline. MODIS has recorded fires since 2000. VIIRS began in 2012, and its sharper sensor detects small fires MODIS misses. Combine them as they are and you get a fake spike in 2012. THERMYX corrects for that by measuring how often MODIS catches the fires VIIRS sees (comparing two satellites, Aqua and S-NPP, that pass over the same place at nearly the same time), finding the fire size above which MODIS is reliable, and then counting only fires at or above that size from both sensors, so every year measures the same thing. It shows Original and Fixed side by side, so anyone can see how much of the jump comes from the instrument change. It covers six regions: California, Amazon, Australia, India, Malaysia, and Canada's boreal forest. Each region has a yearly trend and a daily fire-activity calendar, and every technical term has a plain-English line beneath it.

It gives researchers, journalists, and policymakers a fairer baseline for judging whether fire activity is really changing. In California, the 2012 jump beyond natural variation falls from about +134% to about +20% after correction. Anyone can follow it, because the tool explains its own terms.

Fewer wrong conclusions from long-term fire data. India shows why this matters: many of its fires are small, such as crop-residue burning, and small fires are where the two sensors disagree most. A fair baseline helps people judge whether burning is really changing, and whether programs meant to reduce it are working. Validation against burned-area maps is planned but not yet done, so the results are preliminary. As a sanity check, the pipeline recovered California's biggest fires (Camp, August Complex, Dixie, Caldor) with the right dates and places.

Data: NASA FIRMS, covering MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections

Backend: Python data pipeline (pandas, NumPy, SciPy and PyArrow, tested with pytest). It matches Aqua and S-NPP detections to measure MODIS's catch rate by fire size (with Wilson confidence intervals), compares the 2012 step against a MODIS-only control, and groups detections into fire events by distance and time.

Hosting: the processed data is published as JSON on GitHub Pages

Frontend: React and TypeScript with Vite, built with bun

Design: Bebas Neue, DM Sans, and JetBrains Mono

Workflow: Google AI Studio and GitHub

AI assistants: Claude and Gemini helped with planning, code, design, and writing. All numbers shown come from the pipeline data, not from the AI tools.

Hardware: personal laptops
dataRefs: FIRMS Archive Download (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20 active fire detections)
